Heineken believes that proper disposal of their bottles and cans will help that the festivals sponsored by Heineken and the good times we all enjoy stay clean. TrashAndWin.com, which will be live on the 4th of April 2024, is an innovative platform that encourages people to participate in this endeavour, by giving them tangible exciting rewards.  The platform and its implementation is supported by Ecovidrio and Ecoembes, who are focused on the recycling and environmental management of packaging waste, such as glass bottles and metal beer cans. Ecovidrio and Ecoembes play crucial roles in Spain's commitment to promote recycling, reduce waste, and achieve sustainability goals. They  collaborate with governmental agencies, businesses, and the public to create a circular economy where resources are reused and recycled efficiently. TrashAndWin.com builds on the success of a similar activity undertaken by Heineken Spain in 2023 christened 'Trash Lottery', where physical smart bins were installed at popular music festivals like Monegros and Trui Son Fusteret. These bins treated every piece of litter as a lottery ticket, giving festival goers a chance to win simply by  bringing the trash generated at the festival to the bin installation and disposing of it responsibly. The Trash Lottery initiative by Heineken in 2023, contributed to the collection of 2 tons of glasses, caps, bottles, and plastic items of which the aim is that it will be put into new use. The platform uses an AI trained on trash recycling bins and containers in Spain to enable the phone’s camera to recognise them, making sure that the participant has brought the bottles and cans to the right place. The platform also recognises and treats every piece of Heineken trash as a raffle ticket. Individuals can participate in the raffle simply by  dropping their litter into the correct recycling bins or containers, as an AR filter on TrashAndWin.com instantly announces the results and declares what they have won. The prizes that the participants can win are also determined by processing the location data of the phone and the recycling bin, ensuring that the rewards can be redeemed in the same region.  Ideated by the creative agency LePub and its innovation and tech hub LeGarage, the platform will be first launched in Zaragoza, Spain in collaboration with The Champions Burger event hosted in the city from the 4th to the 14th of April. Participants stand to win passes to Spain’s premier music festivals, UEFA Champions League tickets, dining  experiences at the city’s top restaurants, and other prizes in the weeks leading up to the event.  "We're excited to introduce 'Trash & Win', a one-of-a-kind initiative that merges fun with proper waste management," said Lucia Lopez-Rua Paramo, marketing director, Heineken Spain. "By simply doing their part in keeping their city  tidy, participants don’t just win prizes but also make sure that good times stay responsible, all while trying to win  access to more good times. With each contribution, participants are not only enhancing their event experience but  also becoming an integral part of Heineken's commitment to creating memorable moments responsibly”.'Trash & Win' is set to debut alongside major events throughout Spain, promising an elevated and immersive  experience for those in the cities hosting them. Apart from The Champions Burgers events, Trash&Win will also engage people around music festivals like Festival de les Arts, Arenal Sound, and FIB Benicàssim, seamlessly  blending entertainment with the contribution to keeping event venues and cities clean. In the future, HEINEKEN has the ambition to roll out the 'Trash & Win' platform in more markets, encouraging  consumers to claim rewards simply by disposing of Heineken bottles and cans responsibly. Circular Consumer Behavior
🌎 
Consumption choices greatly impact environmental sustainability and economic efficiency. Traditional consumer behavior typically follows a linear model—purchase, use, and dispose. However, the adoption of circular economy principles, which emphasize reuse, recycling, and responsible consumption, offers a more sustainable alternative.
The accompanying image highlights key decision points in a product’s life cycle, presenting opportunities for shifting towards circular consumer behavior. These decisions not only influence upstream activities such as design and material use but also impact downstream processes like recycling and reuse.
Businesses play a crucial role in facilitating this shift by designing products that are durable, maintainable, and recyclable. By prioritizing these attributes, companies can reduce environmental impacts and support sustainable consumption patterns.
Policymakers can also contribute by creating policies that encourage circular economy practices. This includes implementing regulations that promote recycling, reduce waste, and incentivize companies to develop sustainable products.
For both business strategies and policy interventions, it is essential to consider how these efforts align with the goals of protecting people and the planet. Supporting circular consumer behavior not only addresses environmental challenges but also promotes economic resilience by fostering an efficient use of resources.
This strategic focus on enabling and promoting circular consumer behavior through effective business practices and robust policy frameworks is crucial for the transition to a more sustainable product economy.
Source: European Environment Agency (EEA)

#circulareconomy
#leavenoonebehind 
Introduced by the social scientist Amos Hawley, "ecosystems" are "an arrangement of mutual dependencies in a population by which the whole operates as a unit and thereby maintains a viable environmental relationship." 
In the Circular Economy context, an ecosystem means that all relevant stakeholders along the material flow chain (or loop) must be considered to make circularity a reality.
A circular economy (CE) ecosystem is therefore a system that maintains the flow of materials, products, and resources through restorative and regenerative industrial processes and economic activities. This approach contrasts with the traditional linear economy by emphasising the continuous use of resources, minimising waste, and promoting sustainability.
The key components of a circular economy ecosystem include:
1. Designing for Circularity: Products and materials are designed to last longer, be easily repairable, and recyclable. This involves adopting modular designs and using materials that can be easily separated and recycled.
2. Business Model Innovation: Transitioning to business models such as "product-as-a-service" where products are leased rather than sold, encouraging manufacturers to design for durability and easy maintenance.
3. Collaboration Across Value Chains: Effective circular economies require collaboration across various sectors and industries to design for recycling and disassembly. This includes building hubs for circular innovation where different stakeholders can collaborate and share knowledge.
4. Regeneration of Natural Systems: Businesses can contribute to regenerating natural systems by ensuring that the resources extracted are returned to the environment in a way that restores and enhances ecosystems.
5. Consumer Engagement and Behavior Change: Engaging consumers to adopt circular economy principles in their purchasing and disposal habits is crucial. This involves educating consumers about the benefits of circular products and encouraging behaviors that support a circular economy.
6. Policy and Regulatory Support: Government policies and regulations that support circular economy practices can provide the necessary framework and incentives for businesses to transition. This includes regulations on waste management, recycling standards, and incentives for sustainable practices.
By integrating key components and actors, businesses can not only reduce their environmental impact but also create economic opportunities and improve resource efficiency, leading to a more sustainable and resilient economy.

"Challenging the Idealism: How a Systems Approach Uncovers the Complexities of the Circular Economy"
The circular economy is often seen as a straightforward solution to sustainability, where recycling, reuse, and closed-loop practices naturally reduce waste and maximize resource efficiency. However, when viewed through a systems approach, this idealism is challenged, revealing the complex realities, trade-offs, and structural obstacles that make true circularity far from simple. Here’s how the systems approach reframes the narrative:
1. Revealing Supply Chain Complexities
Although circularity promotes seamless recycling and reuse, a systems perspective exposes the deep complexities within global supply chains. Ensuring every stage of production, distribution, and disposal can handle circular processes requires substantial coordination, often hindered by regional variations in infrastructure and regulations.
These logistical and economic challenges disrupt the simplistic notion that circular solutions can be easily applied acaross industries and geographies.
2. Uncovering Economic Feasibility Issues
Circular models promise cost savings through resource efficiency, but a systems approach shows the often high upfront costs and financial hurdles involved. Designing durable products, investing in closed-loop systems, and scaling recycling technologies can strain budgets, particularly for smaller companies.
3. Exposing Technological Limitations
While a circular economy relies heavily on innovative recycling and material recovery technologies, a systems view shows that existing technologies sometimes fall short. Certain materials, like composites or those with hazardous elements, pose technical and economic challenges that limit recycling feasibility.
4. Factoring in Real-World Consumer and Market Behavior
The systems approach takes consumer behavior and market dynamics into account, revealing that sustainable choices aren’t always a priority. Many consumers prioritize convenience, cost, or brand preference over circular practices, while companies may face pressure to meet immediate market demands.
5. Considering Environmental Trade-Offs
Rather than focusing solely on waste reduction, the systems approach evaluates the total environmental impact of circular practices. Some circular processes, like recycling or repurposing certain materials, may demand high energy or water usage, potentially leading to higher environmental costs.
Conclusion
A systems approach to the circular economy reveals that achieving true circularity is not a simple task. Beyond the idealism, it exposes the need for careful planning, financial investment, technological advancements, behavioral shifts, and supportive policy frameworks. This perspective highlights that a circular economy, rather than being the “easy way out,” demands a realistic and adaptable strategy for sustainability.

Circular opportunities across the product life cycle
🌎 
Circular economy principles present significant opportunities to reduce resource consumption and waste across all stages of a product’s life cycle. This approach goes beyond recycling, emphasizing strategies that extend product life, regenerate natural resources, and minimize environmental impact.
Key actions in circularity include reducing material inputs during the design and manufacturing process, enabling reuse and sharing of products to increase their utilization, and repairing or remanufacturing to extend the functional lifespan of products. Each of these steps aims to limit waste and reduce the need for new resources.
Repairing and remanufacturing, in particular, play a crucial role in keeping products in circulation longer by restoring them to working condition or replacing broken parts. Recycling remains a valuable process, but it is more effective when combined with these upstream actions that prevent waste before it occurs.
Regenerating ecosystems by returning nutrients from materials back to nature also closes the loop on natural resource use. These efforts are not just about waste reduction but also about contributing to a more sustainable and restorative economic system.
Embedding circular strategies into business models is essential for meeting rising sustainability expectations and mitigating the environmental impact of resource-intensive industries. By focusing on life cycle optimization, businesses can drive long-term resilience and contribute to a more sustainable future.
Source: Bain & Company

Circular Economy: A Pathway to Sustainable Growth
In today's world, businesses and industries are increasingly recognizing the need to shift from the traditional linear economy—where we take, make, and dispose—to a circular economy, which focuses on closing the loop through reuse, repair, recycling, and regeneration.
Why Circular Economy Matters:
Reduces Waste:
 
By designing out waste and pollution, we can minimize the environmental impact of products and services from the outset.
Promotes Resource Efficiency: 
Instead of depleting finite resources, we maximize their use and recovery, creating a more resilient system.
Drives Innovation: 
Embracing circularity encourages the development of new technologies, business models, and sustainable materials.
Creates Economic Opportunities:

Design for the end of use
- Not the end of life
- We need objects of infinite utility

Exciting news! There are two new sets of standards that are driving the advancement of the technical aspects of the circular economy and they may apply to your business. 
✅ Yesterday the ISO - International Organization for Standardization released the highly anticipated set of circular economy standards and which cover:
ISO 59004:2024 Circular economy — Vocabulary, principles and guidance for implementation
ISO 59020:2024 Circular economy — Measuring and assessing circularity performance 
ISO 59010:2024 Circular economy — Guidance on the transition of business models and value networks
Read more here: https://lnkd.in/gtQNmP5A 
🇪🇺 There is also the EU's European Sustainability Reporting Standards (which are in the final stages of development and released as a draft presently), ESRS E5 applies to Circular Economy and Resource Use. This is part of the new CSRD reporting requirements which will affect a lot of companies around the world. 
Review the draft standard here: https://lnkd.in/ge7QzQZ3
Correction: Please note on the slides below I say it's still in draft form as I was only able to find the above draft version on the EFRAG website until I was made aware (see comments below) of the published and approved versions here: https://lnkd.in/gbnUs4-8 
🏅Together these new frameworks provide the standardization and technical terminology/approaches needed to ensure that companies everywhere have a clear framework to operate within when adapting to the circular economy.

Moving from a take-make-waste linear economy to one that is circular by design is crucial for business, nature and society to thrive. We welcome ISO’s efforts to bring standardisation to the urgently needed economic shift. The standards provide a helpful global baseline, and practical guidance for companies starting out on their circular economy journey. Yet to truly help businesses to achieve this urgent and ambitious transformation, we would encourage the ISO to raise the bar by:
🏞️ Referencing the regeneration of nature as critical to the circular economy, going beyond protection and the prevention of degradation.
⬆️ placing a greater emphasis on upstream measures such as design and elimination.
🤝 driving harmonisation and streamlining of measurement and reporting by aligning with, or going beyond, existing disclosure frameworks (as set out in the Foundation’s recent review of the reporting landscape).

Here's how to tell your circularity story to consumers
By offering circular models to consumers, brands can become heroes and help people view themselves as eco-friendly. Read More
											By
																																		Suzanne Shelton 
May 23, 2024
Source: Shutterstock/Prinkipo 
I’m facilitating a discussion at Circularity 24 about how to talk about circularity with consumers — to engage them to participate and to drive brand preference and sales. The funny thing is, as we reached out to a few large “house of brands” companies to be part of the discussion, they didn’t feel like they were far enough along the path of actually implementing circular systems, let alone messaging to consumers about them.
There’s both irony and reality at play here. The irony is this:
In our 2023 Global Eco Pulse study we asked people, “Think of someone who you consider to be eco-friendly. Which, if any, of the following describes the person that makes you consider them eco-friendly?” and then we gave a list. All but one of the top five answers were recycling and reuse behaviors. This matters because well over half of people around the world want to be seen as someone who engages in eco-friendly behaviors/purchases. So, offering consumers circular models is a way for brands to be heroes and help people manifest themselves as the eco-friendly people they want to be seen as.
In our 2022 Eco Pulse study, we asked people in America who ranked themselves as “extremely concerned” about plastics in the ocean how much it would relieve their concerns about plastics if they were easier to reuse. Twenty-nine percent said entirely and 63 percent said somewhat. So circular business models are a key way to turn perceptions of plastics around — the petrochemical industry and the plastics packaging industry should be all over this!
And that gets us to the realities. Changing from a single use, linear way of doing things is HARD. Imagine you’re a brand that sells a consumable such as lotion or cookies. In order for a consumer to buy the lotion or cookies in a reusable format, there have to be dispensaries installed in the stores where they shop. We probably can’t rely on everyone to bring their own containers (likely with a deposit), so there has to be a way to take a container and bring it back, which then places a burden of cleaning the container on the retailer.
Starbucks is out in front on this — they recently expanded a reusable cup pilot to all their stores in the U.S. and Canada. I hope we’ll get to hear from them on lessons learned, and I hope other quick-serve chains will follow suit. The bigger challenge, though, remains retail.
If we’re going to implement circular systems at scale in everyday consumer experiences, brands, their suppliers, and retailers will have to work together to align on delivery systems that work. The Body Shop has been “going there” for a couple of years and likely has a lot to share/teach other retailers. Here’s a great piece with some insights.
Bottom line: People are interested in waste-free shopping. They want what it will say about them/allow themselves to project to the world, and they want it to be convenient. I say, give the people what they want! Work together to make it happen, tell the story of how you’re doing it, what you’re learning, and drive brand preference as a result.

Close dialog All work  All work Glass to GardenMaker's Mark© 2023An experiential marketing program designed to crush it.The ChallengeMaker’s Mark, the world’s largest B Corp distillery, was looking for a way to reduce its glass bottle packaging waste, but people have become disillusioned by traditional recycling – learning a lot of it actually ends up in landfills.The SolutionInstead of simply encouraging people to throw bottles into bins that might lead to landfills, we let them pulverize the bottles (even those of competitors) at local grocery stores – turning them into a reusable soil mix that went to local community gardens to help grow food. For the experience, we placed portable glass pulverizers in Kroger stores and created a full retail campaign that led to crushing our sustainability goals.CommsPlan:Encouraging ParticipationThe Glass to Garden campaign ran across seven locations of the nation’s largest grocery chain. We designed and placed mass displays, promotional posters and recyclable totes in the participating Kroger stores where we held pulverizing events and sampling activations every week. Local media coverage garnered by our PR team encouraged consumers to save and bring their empty bottles to the events where they could help crush the glass and receive a complimentary bourbon tasting.CreativeExecution:Beautiful SustainabilityThe creative executions showed the iconic Maker’s Mark bottle beautifully crushed and broken – designed to turn heads and pique curiosity of the next generation of whisky drinkers (25+) who value sustainability and protecting the environment. The experience ​​made them participants in the sustainability vision of Maker’s Mark and let them become active contributors to a better, greener community.Take a LookBehind the ScenesHow do you handle a photoshoot with a pile of broken glass? Circular Economy Glossary
🔄 
The Ellen MacArthur Foundation's glossary on the circular economy serves as a fundamental resource to foster a comprehensive grasp of pivotal concepts across various sectors. 
This tool is tailored to enhance the understanding of essential terms like recycle, reverse logistics, and finite resources, delineating the nuances between virgin, non-virgin, and renewable materials, as well as biological and technical cycles, including reuse, refurbishment, and remanufacturing.
This glossary is a step towards simplifying the intricate vernacular of the circular economy, aiming to bridge gaps in comprehension and application. 
By solidifying a shared lexicon and illuminating terms that are frequently misinterpreted, the Foundation facilitates a streamlined approach for entities ranging from businesses to urban governance, to not only conceptualize but effectively implement circular economy models.
The utility of this glossary extends beyond mere clarification. It is an aid for internal understanding within organizations, supports collaborative ventures, enriches dialogue, and is instrumental in crafting informed reports, strategic planning, and communications. 
Accessibility to such knowledge is crucial for stakeholders to orchestrate and align their practices with the principles of circularity, driving the global economy towards sustainable transformation.

I just completed the Ellen MacArthur Foundation Circular Economy online course and can highly recommend if you want a good understanding of what the circular economy is and how it can make your business a force for good. 
The circular economy has three core principles: 
1. Eliminate waste and pollution
2. Keep products and materials in use
3. Regenerate natural systems 
This circular approach will enable us to move from current linear take, make, dispose businesses and lifestyles that have caused significant harm to planet, nature and people, to a circular system that keeps us well within planetary boundaries, provides resilience and abundance in our food systems, creates positive impactful businesses, removes waste, increases job opportunities and supports fair and just societies.
The circular economy is built using a biomimicry approach replicating natural systems where everything is circulated and nothing is wasted. Using two cycles - biological and technical - it provides strategy to employ closed loop systems that keep products and components in the system through regeneration and replenishment (biological cycle) and remanufacture and refurbishment (technical cycle), with materials and components always maintaining the highest value, and recycling as a last resort.

I've just come across these incredible insights from Vojtech Vosecky, who had the privilege of learning from the legend of the circular economy - William McDonough. These lessons aren’t just words, they’re a call to action for anyone passionate about sustainability! Let’s break this down and ignite change together! 🚀💡
1. Design for the End of Use, Not the End of Life 
👉 Imagine if every product had infinite utility. What if nothing we made was ever truly wasted? Stop thinking about an ‘end of life’ - there is no end. Redesign your mindset for the end of use, and create a cycle of endless value. Let’s elevate our imagination!
2. Forget ‘Net Zero’ – Focus on Doing Good! 
✅ Listen, reducing harm isn’t enough. You’ve got to make a shift from ‘being less bad’ to being actively good. Challenge yourself and your organization: What can we do today that leaves a positive legacy? Stop settling for zero - aim for abundance!
3. Offsets Are Scary – Let’s Inset Instead 🌿 💡 
Offsetting CO2 can be a trap, like putting a Band-Aid on a wound without treating the source. Instead, let’s insert value right at the origin of the problem. Create regenerative cycles - because thriving is what nature is all about.
4. Start with Values, Not Targets 🎯 ⚡ 
Targets are essential, but where’s your foundation? It starts with values. Values give birth to a vision, and from there, you build your strategy, your actions, and then your KPIs. Know who you are and why you do what you do. Make those values crystal clear, and everything else will follow.
5. It’s Not Hard to Abate – It’s Hard to Stop, Think, and Design 
🛑💭 🔑 Here’s the truth: Stopping is hard. Thinking deeply, challenging the status quo, and designing with intention - that’s the tough part. But when you do, breakthroughs happen. Don’t rush blindly into solutions. Give yourself permission to slow down and create greatness.
🔥 These 5 lessons aren't just for the circular economy - they’re for LIFE. Adopt them. Apply them. And let’s build a world that doesn’t just survive... but thrives. 🌍💚
Now, it's YOUR turn—what action will you take today to be not just ‘less bad,’ but actively GOOD? Let’s go out there and make the impact we know we can! 🚀💪

Circular Economy
These workshops offer an alternative to throwaway culture
Repair clinics bring power to the people. Here’s why businesses should care. Read More
											By
																																		Kori Goldberg 
February 16, 2024
Participants tackle a coffee maker at a repair cafe in Europe in 2021. Credit: Repair Cafe 
Although disposability often reigns supreme in our culture, local repair clinics are slowing down consumption and prioritizing the practice of repair, fostering principles of the circular economy. In Berlin, London and New York, they have become commonplace. These educational and hands-on workshops, offered at libraries, schools and local government offices, bring together communities while extending the lifespans of products.
“There are more repair cafes than ever before,” Elizabeth Chamberlain, director of sustainability at the global repair organization iFixit, said via email. “Repair cafes help fill the void left by the decline of the independent repair market.”
In California, Fixit Clinic is leading the way, started by right-to-repair advocate Peter Mui in 2009. Its volunteer staffers help to disassemble, troubleshoot and repair a wide variety of broken items for free, including computers, clocks, clothing, bicycles and kitchen gadgets. What began as a small initiative has grown into a movement: 200 Fixit Clinics were held across the United States in 2023.
Connections for communities
Grassroots community repair efforts around the world share similar goals. Dutch journalist Martine Postma organized her first Repair Cafe in Amsterdam in 2009. The decentralized network now has 3,009 free-repair cafes from Japan to Iceland to Brazil. Tools, materials and about 45,240 skilled volunteers help mend an estimated 54,288 items per month. The organization promises at least an attempt to repair anything that “you can manage to carry on your own to the Repair Cafe.” 
Both Fixit Clinic and Repair Cafe offer resources to help organizers recruit experts, engage community and kickstart recurring workshops.
 
GreenBiz Group
Image Title Text
A bulletin board sign for a repair cafe in Evanston, Illinois, in February.
media_caption
A bulletin board sign for a repair cafe in Evanston, Illinois, in February.
Repair clinics serve as vibrant hubs for community engagement and connection. Organizers often strive for broader, less tangible goals than maximizing the numbers of items fixed: instilling confidence and equipping people with critical thinking skills to repair independently. 
Chamberlain underscored the value of skill-building and self-sufficiency. Often people who show up at repair clinics to watch and learn eventually become experts in their own right, she said. 
Implications for businesses
The rise of repair initiatives carries significant implications for corporate sustainability practitioners. Ultra-fast fashion companies such as Shein and e-commerce platforms such as Temu are escalating low-quality, high-consumption habits. Repair clinics offer a different ethos and different habits.
Businesses have many options to meet and support this movement. They can foster an ecosystem of repair by supporting right to repair legislation; designing for modularity, durability and standardization; and providing accessible parts and repair manuals. Companies can also send their repair experts to local events to share best-practices.  
“At repair cafes, everyone’s favorite devices to work on are the ones with lots of clear troubleshooting information and readily available parts,” says Chamberlain. “The best repair documentation goes beyond just describing how to replace parts and actually includes schematics and wiring diagrams.”
Companies committed to enabling the circular economy should also consider supporting and participating in these community-driven repair initiatives. Last year, a repair event organized by and for HP employees in Boise, Idaho, prompted conversations about the repairability of the company’s own laptops and printers. By hosting repair clinics, companies can demonstrate their commitment to sustainability while engaging with communities. 
Embracing repair initiatives often aligns with existing corporate circularity goals and can enhance brand reputation and customer loyalty. Businesses that champion repairability and promote sustainable consumption can position themselves as leaders and forge deeper connections with their customers, ultimately contributing to the emergence of a more circular economy.

Circular processing ladder
🌎 
The Circular Processing Ladder is a fundamental concept that guides sustainable practices by emphasizing a hierarchy of strategies aimed at minimizing waste and maximizing resource efficiency. 
This model offers a roadmap from the most preferred outcome of "Refuse" to the least preferred but still necessary "Recover," ensuring every aspect of product life-cycle management contributes to a more sustainable world.
Refuse: At the pinnacle of the ladder, the strategy is to make a product redundant by either abandoning its original function or by finding alternative ways to achieve the same function. This step is crucial as it encourages designing products and systems that eliminate the need for excess materials from the outset.
Rethink and Reduce: These steps focus on optimizing the use and production of goods. "Rethink" involves making the product use more intensive, either by sharing it among a larger number of users or by enhancing its functionality. "Reduce" seeks to improve the efficiency of production processes and to use fewer raw materials for the same output, effectively lowering the environmental footprint.
Reuse and Repair: Directly below, "Reuse" involves allowing a discarded yet functional product to serve its original purpose for a different user. This prolongs the product's life and reduces the need for new products. "Repair" extends this idea by fixing defective products to preserve their functionality, thus supporting sustainability through maintenance rather than disposal.
Refurbish and Remanufacture: "Refurbish" entails updating old products to modern standards, making them relevant and useful longer. "Remanufacture" takes this a step further by using functioning components of old products to create new ones, which is especially relevant in industries like electronics and automotive, where many parts can find new life in new products.
Repurpose and Recycle: At the lower end of the ladder, "Repurpose" involves altering a product or its components to serve a new function, which is an innovative way to reduce waste. Following this, "Recycle" involves processing used materials to create new products, which helps to conserve raw materials and reduce energy consumption, completing the loop of a circular economy.
These steps, together, form a cohesive approach to managing products and resources in a manner that significantly reduces waste and encourages the reuse of materials, aligning with global sustainability goals.

Steps to build a circular economy
🌎 
In the journey towards sustainability, transitioning from a linear to a circular economy is key. The circular model challenges the traditional 'take-make-dispose' approach and fosters innovation, efficiency, and responsible consumption. A roadmap highlighting essential steps helps to achieve a circular economy effectively.
ReFUSE is the starting point, focusing on rethinking consumption habits. Refusing products with limited or unnecessary functions curbs waste at the source. This proactive step addresses waste prevention by limiting the production and consumption of items that do not add significant value.
ReTHINK involves redesigning products to be multifunctional, promoting more intensive and prolonged use. This approach supports the creation of adaptable products that meet multiple needs, extending their utility and minimizing the need for new resources. ReDUCE follows by enhancing manufacturing and design efficiency through eco-design principles, ensuring that resource use and waste generation are minimized.
ReCOVER focuses on the collection, disassembly, and sorting of high-value materials from used products, preparing them for reintegration into production. ReUSE encourages the continued use of products by enabling them to be utilized by new users, effectively extending their lifecycle and delaying disposal.
RePAIR and ReFURBISH are essential for maintaining products in use. Repairing products ensures they remain functional, while refurbishment updates them to current standards, prolonging their market viability. ReMANUFACTURE takes this further by using parts of discarded products to create new ones, reducing the need for virgin materials. RePURPOSE innovatively applies parts of old products to new uses, diversifying their utility and application.
ReCYCLE concludes the process by reclaiming value from materials and keeping them in circulation. The transition to a circular economy requires these practices alongside socio-institutional change and responsible resource management. This approach minimizes new resource extraction, mitigates environmental impacts, and fosters a regenerative economic system where waste is continuously minimized and value reintroduced.
#circulareconomy #sustainability #innovation #sustainable #business #esg #climateaction

Circular Economy Terminologies
🔄 
In the face of mounting environmental challenges, the transition to a circular economy has become an imperative for both planetary health and societal well-being. This economy is defined by systems and processes that aim to eliminate waste, circulate resources, and regenerate natural systems. 
Here, ten critical concepts underpin this transformative approach:
▪ Circular Economy: A regenerative system where products and materials are kept in use, mimicking natural ecosystems where waste serves as a resource.
▪ Closed-loop System: Emphasizes the continuous reuse and recycling of resources, reducing the need for new resource extraction and minimizing waste.
▪ Cradle-to-Cradle Design: Focuses on the entire lifecycle of products, from material sourcing to end-of-life disposal, ensuring perpetual recyclability or upcycling without loss of quality.
▪ Extended Producer Responsibility: Holds producers accountable for the environmental impact of their products across the lifecycle, including disposal and recycling.
▪ Product-as-a-Service (PaaS): A model where access to a product or service is sold rather than the physical product itself, encouraging durability and recyclability.
▪ Regenerative Design: Aims to create systems that restore ecosystems and resources, going beyond minimizing harm to enhancing environmental health.
▪ Upcycling: Transforms waste materials into new products of higher value or quality, adding value to the original material rather than breaking it down.
▪ Circular Procurement: Involves purchasing practices that prioritize products and services with high environmental and social performance, including circularity.
▪ Circular Business Models: Innovative business approaches that emphasize resource efficiency, sustainability, and the circular flow of materials.
▪ Circular Design: The practice of designing products and systems with circular principles, considering durability, reparability, and end-of-life recyclability.
The urgency for a shift towards a circular economy is clear; it presents a systemic solution to reduce waste, enhance sustainability, and promote a harmonious relationship between people and the planet. This shift requires reimagining traditional business models, product designs, and consumer behaviors to prioritize resource efficiency, sustainability, and the well-being of ecosystems.
Adopting a circular economy not only addresses the pressing environmental issues of today but also fosters innovation, economic growth, and resilience. It challenges businesses and individuals to rethink how products are designed, used, and reused, ensuring that materials circulate within the economy without entering the environment as waste.

Building a Circular Economy: It Starts with Avoidance.
In the journey toward a sustainable future, the circular economy shifts us from a “produce-consume-dispose” cycle to a system focused on preserving resources at every stage. 
The most impactful step? Avoidance — the principle of eliminating waste before it happens. The circular economy operates on principles that prioritize reducing waste and maximizing the value of resources. It starts with Refuse (Avoid) — avoiding unnecessary products altogether. Rethink and Reduce then guide how we design products: aiming for multifunctional use and resource efficiency. 
Next, Reuse, Repair, and Refurbish extend a product’s life, keeping it in circulation as long as possible.
When items reach the end of their current use, Repurpose, Remanufacture, and Recycle help reclaim materials for new purposes.
By embracing these principles, we shift from a disposable mindset to one that continuously regenerates and retains value.
At Carrot, we create high-value avoidance credits that incentivize responsible consumption, starting where it matters most: stopping waste at its source. 
Avoidance credits lead the circular economy hierarchy by cutting emissions and reducing demand for new materials, making them the gold standard for impact and sustainability. Through avoidance credits, we not only minimize environmental footprints but also pave the way for innovation, helping businesses meet their goals while building a regenerative future.

🔄🌍The circular economy plays a pivotal role in creating a sustainable future by fundamentally reshaping how resources are utilized, managed, and circulated within society. Unlike the traditional linear economy, which follows a "take-make-dispose" model, the circular economy aims to minimize waste and maximize resource efficiency by promoting three key principles:
1️⃣ Resource Conservation: In a circular economy, resources are kept in use for as long as possible through strategies such as repair, refurbishment, and remanufacturing. This prolongs the lifespan of products and materials, reducing the need for virgin resources and minimizing environmental degradation associated with extraction and production.
2️⃣ Closed-Loop Systems: Circular economy principles emphasize the importance of creating closed-loop systems where materials are continuously reused, recycled, or repurposed at the end of their life cycles. This not only reduces the volume of waste sent to landfills but also conserves valuable resources and reduces the environmental footprint of manufacturing processes.
3️⃣ Regenerative Practices: Beyond waste reduction and resource efficiency, the circular economy promotes regenerative practices that contribute to ecosystem restoration and resilience. By prioritizing renewable resources, designing products for biodegradability, and embracing nature-inspired solutions, the circular economy seeks to restore ecosystems and mitigate the impacts of climate change.
The circular economy transforms our approach to resources, promoting longevity, closed-loop systems, and regenerative practices.                         Paris 2024 Gives First Look at Its Circular Approach to Olympic Games
                    
Focusing on the material footprint of the upcoming summer Games, Paris 2024 is
leaning heavily into recycled materials and plans for reuse of all temporary
infrastructure, furniture and equipment.
                        
                        
                                                                            
                                                Published 8 months ago | About a 5 minute read
                    
                        Image: Paris 2024
This week, Paris 2024 unveiled the first results
of its circular economy strategy for this summer’s Olympic Games. Integrated
into every level of the organization, the strategy is based on three key
principles: organizing the Games with fewer resources, making better use of
these resources by promoting eco-design and ensuring the second life of
resources after the Games. For all the facilities, Paris 2024 has proposed a
more responsible model: thinking about their post-Games life before the Games
even start.
Tokyo 2020 were the first Games to implement circular principles — through
initiatives including medals podiums made from post-consumer recycled plastic
materials
and medals made from recycled consumer
electronics.
Paris 2024 aims to take this further, with circularity woven into every possible
aspect of the event.
Assessing and reducing the Games’ ‘material footprint’
From spectator seating, tents, beds, chairs and tables to tennis balls,
shuttlecocks, flags, bibs and so much more, organizing the world's largest
international sporting event requires a vast amount of equipment and many
resources.
As with its carbon footprint, which Paris 2024 has controversially
proclaimed
will be half that of previous Games, the organization wanted to calculate its
“material footprint” in advance of the Games, i.e. the sum of the weight of all
the resources mobilized for the needs of the Games — a first in the history of
the Olympic and Paralympic Games. Venue by venue, Paris 2024 has produced a
detailed map of the resources needed to organize the Games with the aim of
reducing and pooling resources and controlling their life cycle before, during
and after the Games.
Regarding suppliers, Paris 2024 applied its Responsible Purchasing
Strategy —
of which circularity is one of the pillars. In its calls for tender, Paris 2024
has given preference to suppliers who:
adopt an eco-design approach to their products and services,
give priority to equipment hire and long-life products,
use lower-impact raw materials such as recycled materials or production
offcuts,
are committed to certification processes,
offer solutions for the second and end-of-life of products (reuse,
recycling),
minimize the use of packaging and promote reusable or recyclable packaging.
To date, thanks to the application of this Responsible Purchasing Strategy, 90
percent of the six million resource elements used will be deployed and taken
over by the Games' service providers and partners, who manage a large proportion
of the services required to organize the Games. The remaining 10 percent of
resources will be the direct responsibility of Paris 2024, as the Organizing
Committee.
Organizing an event with fewer resources
At the time of the bid, Paris 2024 proposed a concept for a more responsible
Games: capitalizing on 95 percent of existing infrastructure or temporary
venues, to build less and thus mobilize fewer resources.
This principle of reducing resources is also reflected in the interior design of
the ~40 competition and non-competition venues. By evaluating and pooling its
needs whenever possible, Paris 2024 says it has been able to reduce the amount
of furniture and signage needed from 800,000 to 600,000.
In addition to reducing its needs, Paris 2024 has given preference to hiring
rather than buying from event organizers. Of the two million pieces of sporting
equipment, three-quarters will be hired or made available by sports federations,
along with 75 percent of electronic equipment including televisions, computers
and printers. Finally, with Official Partner GL Events; as well as
Arena, ES Global and Loxam — Official Supporters for temporary
infrastructure and fitting out — 100 percent of the stands, tents and bungalows
to be used will be hired rather than purchased.
Regarding catering, Paris 2024 has committed to reducing single-use plastic by
50 percent compared to the Games of London 2012 by using returnable, recycled
and reused containers. To achieve this, Worldwide Partner Coca-Cola will
offer packaging-free beverages by installing drinks fountains where the
configuration of the venue allows to significantly reduce the use of plastic
bottles.
More resource-efficient design
The second pillar of Paris 2024’s circular economy strategy is promoting
eco-design. With respect to dressing competition and non-competition venues;
installing signage; or furnishing spectator, athlete and volunteer areas, the
eco-design approach to products has been a key evaluation criterion in Paris
2024's calls for tenders.
For the flooring for the handball, volleyball and sitting volleyball events, as
well as wheelchair basketball, wheelchair rugby, goalball and boccia, Paris 2024
chose Gerflor — a French company specializing in
floor coverings. The 33,466 m² of sports flooring supplied by Gerflor will
contain an average of 35 percent recycled materials and will be 100 percent
recyclable; and Gerflor is committed to finding a reuse destination in sports or
educational establishments after the competition, for all the flooring used
during the Paris 2024 Games.
To furnish the competition venues, the Athletes' Village and the Media Village,
Official Supporter RGS Events has sourced certain lots of furniture from
companies in the Social and Solidarity
Economy
(SSE) sector, with the support of the Les Canaux
association as part of the SSE 2024 program. The athletes' areas will feature
coffee tables made from recycled shuttlecocks, poufs made from parachute canvas
and chairs made from recycled bottle caps. As for the athletes' beds, Official
Supporter Airweave has chosen to manufacture the base
frames in France from 100 percent recycled cardboard, and to recycle them in
France after the event.
100% second life for temporary infrastructure, furniture and equipment
By their very nature, the Olympic and Paralympic Games are ephemeral events. To
ensure that the resources mobilized for the Games can be reused and do not
become waste, Paris 2024 thought about the second life of material assets before
the event. As with eco-design, the organization chose suppliers that incorporate
second life into their products.
For example, Official Supporter Sodexo
Live! will produce the 35,000
plates to be used in the Athletes' Village restaurant without a logo to
facilitate their reuse. Also in the Athletes' Village, Official Supporter
Saint-Gobain has developed partitions that can be reused to convert
athletes' rooms into housing or to be reinstalled on other sites. Materials and
temporary structures (tents, stands and bungalows) will be reused or recycled.
The second life of the Games' facilities also involves the legacy left by such
facilities to the regions and the world of sport. In particular, the Organizing
Committee has decided to bequeath the temporary swimming pools used during the
Games to the Seine-Saint-Denis region for use by the local community.

Circular Economy Glossary
🔄 
The Ellen MacArthur Foundation's glossary on the circular economy serves as a fundamental resource to foster a comprehensive grasp of pivotal concepts across various sectors. 
This tool is tailored to enhance the understanding of essential terms like recycle, reverse logistics, and finite resources, delineating the nuances between virgin, non-virgin, and renewable materials, as well as biological and technical cycles, including reuse, refurbishment, and remanufacturing.
This glossary is a step towards simplifying the intricate vernacular of the circular economy, aiming to bridge gaps in comprehension and application. 
By solidifying a shared lexicon and illuminating terms that are frequently misinterpreted, the Foundation facilitates a streamlined approach for entities ranging from businesses to urban governance, to not only conceptualize but effectively implement circular economy models.
The utility of this glossary extends beyond mere clarification. It is an aid for internal understanding within organizations, supports collaborative ventures, enriches dialogue, and is instrumental in crafting informed reports, strategic planning, and communications. 
Accessibility to such knowledge is crucial for stakeholders to orchestrate and align their practices with the principles of circularity, driving the global economy towards sustainable transformation.

I just completed the Ellen MacArthur Foundation Circular Economy online course and can highly recommend if you want a good understanding of what the circular economy is and how it can make your business a force for good. 
The circular economy has three core principles: 
1. Eliminate waste and pollution
2. Keep products and materials in use
3. Regenerate natural systems 
This circular approach will enable us to move from current linear take, make, dispose businesses and lifestyles that have caused significant harm to planet, nature and people, to a circular system that keeps us well within planetary boundaries, provides resilience and abundance in our food systems, creates positive impactful businesses, removes waste, increases job opportunities and supports fair and just societies.
The circular economy is built using a biomimicry approach replicating natural systems where everything is circulated and nothing is wasted. Using two cycles - biological and technical - it provides strategy to employ closed loop systems that keep products and components in the system through regeneration and replenishment (biological cycle) and remanufacture and refurbishment (technical cycle), with materials and components always maintaining the highest value, and recycling as a last resort.

I’ve finally met the legend of the circular economy - William McDonough. Here are his 5 lessons for everyone in sustainability: 
1. Design for the end of use
- Not the end of life
- We need objects of infinite utility
2. Forget the ‘net zero’
- Stop being less bad
- focus on doing good
3. Offsets are scary
- offseting CO2 is a dead end
- let’s inset instead
4. Start with values, not targets
- values -> vision -> strategy -> KPIs
- not the other way around
5. It’s not hard to abate
- it’s hard to stop, think and design
- so let’s go ahead and do it!
Which one is your favorite? 
We’ve met at Regeneration.VC ‘s annual event, Reassembly. Definitely a highlight of my whole week in NYC!

I've just come across these incredible insights from Vojtech Vosecky, who had the privilege of learning from the legend of the circular economy - William McDonough. These lessons aren’t just words, they’re a call to action for anyone passionate about sustainability! Let’s break this down and ignite change together! 🚀💡
1. Design for the End of Use, Not the End of Life 
👉 Imagine if every product had infinite utility. What if nothing we made was ever truly wasted? Stop thinking about an ‘end of life’ - there is no end. Redesign your mindset for the end of use, and create a cycle of endless value. Let’s elevate our imagination!
2. Forget ‘Net Zero’ – Focus on Doing Good! 
✅ Listen, reducing harm isn’t enough. You’ve got to make a shift from ‘being less bad’ to being actively good. Challenge yourself and your organization: What can we do today that leaves a positive legacy? Stop settling for zero - aim for abundance!
3. Offsets Are Scary – Let’s Inset Instead 🌿 💡 
Offsetting CO2 can be a trap, like putting a Band-Aid on a wound without treating the source. Instead, let’s insert value right at the origin of the problem. Create regenerative cycles - because thriving is what nature is all about.
4. Start with Values, Not Targets 🎯 ⚡ 
Targets are essential, but where’s your foundation? It starts with values. Values give birth to a vision, and from there, you build your strategy, your actions, and then your KPIs. Know who you are and why you do what you do. Make those values crystal clear, and everything else will follow.
5. It’s Not Hard to Abate – It’s Hard to Stop, Think, and Design 
🛑💭 🔑 Here’s the truth: Stopping is hard. Thinking deeply, challenging the status quo, and designing with intention - that’s the tough part. But when you do, breakthroughs happen. Don’t rush blindly into solutions. Give yourself permission to slow down and create greatness.
🔥 These 5 lessons aren't just for the circular economy - they’re for LIFE. Adopt them. Apply them. And let’s build a world that doesn’t just survive... but thrives. 🌍💚
Now, it's YOUR turn—what action will you take today to be not just ‘less bad,’ but actively GOOD? Let’s go out there and make the impact we know we can! 🚀💪

Circular Economy
These workshops offer an alternative to throwaway culture
Repair clinics bring power to the people. Here’s why businesses should care. Read More
											By
																																		Kori Goldberg 
February 16, 2024
Participants tackle a coffee maker at a repair cafe in Europe in 2021. Credit: Repair Cafe 
Although disposability often reigns supreme in our culture, local repair clinics are slowing down consumption and prioritizing the practice of repair, fostering principles of the circular economy. In Berlin, London and New York, they have become commonplace. These educational and hands-on workshops, offered at libraries, schools and local government offices, bring together communities while extending the lifespans of products.
“There are more repair cafes than ever before,” Elizabeth Chamberlain, director of sustainability at the global repair organization iFixit, said via email. “Repair cafes help fill the void left by the decline of the independent repair market.”
In California, Fixit Clinic is leading the way, started by right-to-repair advocate Peter Mui in 2009. Its volunteer staffers help to disassemble, troubleshoot and repair a wide variety of broken items for free, including computers, clocks, clothing, bicycles and kitchen gadgets. What began as a small initiative has grown into a movement: 200 Fixit Clinics were held across the United States in 2023.
Connections for communities
Grassroots community repair efforts around the world share similar goals. Dutch journalist Martine Postma organized her first Repair Cafe in Amsterdam in 2009. The decentralized network now has 3,009 free-repair cafes from Japan to Iceland to Brazil. Tools, materials and about 45,240 skilled volunteers help mend an estimated 54,288 items per month. The organization promises at least an attempt to repair anything that “you can manage to carry on your own to the Repair Cafe.” 
Both Fixit Clinic and Repair Cafe offer resources to help organizers recruit experts, engage community and kickstart recurring workshops.
 
GreenBiz Group
Image Title Text
A bulletin board sign for a repair cafe in Evanston, Illinois, in February.
media_caption
A bulletin board sign for a repair cafe in Evanston, Illinois, in February.
Repair clinics serve as vibrant hubs for community engagement and connection. Organizers often strive for broader, less tangible goals than maximizing the numbers of items fixed: instilling confidence and equipping people with critical thinking skills to repair independently. 
Chamberlain underscored the value of skill-building and self-sufficiency. Often people who show up at repair clinics to watch and learn eventually become experts in their own right, she said. 
Implications for businesses
The rise of repair initiatives carries significant implications for corporate sustainability practitioners. Ultra-fast fashion companies such as Shein and e-commerce platforms such as Temu are escalating low-quality, high-consumption habits. Repair clinics offer a different ethos and different habits.
Businesses have many options to meet and support this movement. They can foster an ecosystem of repair by supporting right to repair legislation; designing for modularity, durability and standardization; and providing accessible parts and repair manuals. Companies can also send their repair experts to local events to share best-practices.  
“At repair cafes, everyone’s favorite devices to work on are the ones with lots of clear troubleshooting information and readily available parts,” says Chamberlain. “The best repair documentation goes beyond just describing how to replace parts and actually includes schematics and wiring diagrams.”
Companies committed to enabling the circular economy should also consider supporting and participating in these community-driven repair initiatives. Last year, a repair event organized by and for HP employees in Boise, Idaho, prompted conversations about the repairability of the company’s own laptops and printers. By hosting repair clinics, companies can demonstrate their commitment to sustainability while engaging with communities. 
Embracing repair initiatives often aligns with existing corporate circularity goals and can enhance brand reputation and customer loyalty. Businesses that champion repairability and promote sustainable consumption can position themselves as leaders and forge deeper connections with their customers, ultimately contributing to the emergence of a more circular economy.

Circular economy system
🔄 
The circular economy is a transformative system where materials are designed to never become waste, and natural ecosystems are actively regenerated. This approach is vital in maintaining products and materials in use at their highest utility and value through continuous cycles of maintenance, reuse, refurbishment, remanufacture, recycling, and composting. 
By prioritizing these processes, the circular economy directly tackles global challenges such as climate change, biodiversity loss, waste, and pollution, effectively decoupling economic activity from the consumption of finite resources.
This sustainable model operates on three core principles that are embedded in the design stage: eliminating waste and pollution, circulating products and materials at their highest value, and regenerating nature. 
The foundation of this system is a shift toward renewable energy and materials, fortifying a resilient economic framework that is advantageous for businesses, individuals, and the environment.
The diagram visualizes this integrated model, mapping out a path that reduces the need for extracting and importing natural resources, and diminishes reliance on detrimental processes such as incineration and landfilling. The focus is on optimizing resource use, minimizing emissions, and developing energy-efficient strategies across the lifecycle of products.
Adoption of the circular economy model offers a route to innovation and resilience for all sectors, aligning economic activity with the imperative of environmental preservation. It is not just a strategy for minimizing harm but an actionable plan for regenerative growth, where every element is designed to contribute to a healthy, sustainable world.
Source: European Environment Agency

♻ Ever heard about the R-strategies or circular economy?
Inside every machine, product, or process are countless essential resources with a big ecological and social footprint:
>> 90% of biodiversity loss is caused by resource extraction and processing
>> Up to 80% of products’ environmental impacts are determined at the design phase
>> 11.8% the current circular material use rate in the EU
Circular Economy outlines how we can reduce the amount of resources for anything we design, manufacture and decommission. It enables us to tackle climate change, biodiversity loss and social needs while promoting resilience and sustainability:
R0 = Reduce - consume less
R1 = Reduce – use less materials
R2 = Resell, Reuse – 2n hand market
R3 = Repair – extend lifetime, same user
R4 = Refurbish – extend lifetime, new user
R5 = Remanufacture – of product components in new, similar product
R6 = Repurpose – of product components, in other function
R7 = Recycle materials – downcycle, recycle, upcycle
R8 = Recover energy – incinerate, but store/ use energy
R9 = Re-mine – mine materials in landfills
And the great thing is that you can apply it for business and private purposes.

The right kind of circles to go around in! Insights from the Evolution of Sustainability Event: Advancing Circular Economy. 
 
We were thrilled to attend the Evolution of Sustainability event during London Climate Action Week, where thought leaders, innovators, and industry experts gathered to discuss the future of sustainability. The event was a rich source of inspiration, highlighting the importance of embracing circular economy principles and exploring innovative strategies to minimize electronic waste. 
 
What is the Circular Economy? 
 
The circular economy is an economic system aimed at eliminating waste and the continual use of resources. It encompasses a transition to renewable energy sources, the redesign of materials, products, and systems to ensure they can be reused, repaired, and recycled. This approach contrasts sharply with the traditional linear economy, which often leads to significant environmental degradation and resource depletion. 
 
By designing products with their end-of-life in mind, the circular economy reduces the volume of waste sent to landfills and incinerators. Products are designed to be disassembled and reused, minimizing waste generation. 
 
By minimizing waste and promoting the reuse of materials, the circular economy reduces pollution associated with waste disposal and resource extraction. This includes a reduction in greenhouse gas emissions and lower levels of soil, water, and air pollution. 
 
Reducing the need for new raw materials helps to protect ecosystems and biodiversity. By limiting deforestation, mining, and other extractive activities, the circular economy helps preserve natural habitats. 
 
The shift towards a circular economy drives innovation in product design, manufacturing processes, and business models. Companies that adopt circular practices can differentiate themselves in the market, gaining a competitive edge. 
 
By reducing dependence on raw materials and promoting the reuse of existing resources, companies can mitigate risks associated with resource scarcity and supply chain disruptions. This enhances business resilience and stability. 
Potential for Growth 
 
The circular economy offers a compelling vision for a sustainable and profitable future. By redesigning systems to keep resources in use for as long as possible, we can reduce waste, conserve resources, and create economic opportunities. Embracing the circular economy is not just an environmental imperative; it is a strategic advantage for businesses looking to thrive in the 21st century.

Reducing Our Carbon Footprint: Practical Steps for a More Sustainable Future
In an increasingly environmentally conscious world, it's crucial for each of us to take responsibility for reducing our carbon footprint. But what exactly is the carbon footprint, and how can we contribute to reducing it?
The carbon footprint is the total amount of greenhouse gases, especially carbon dioxide (CO2), released into the atmosphere as a direct or indirect result of human activities. From the energy we consume to the food we choose, our daily actions have an impact on the environment.
So, how can we do our part to reduce our carbon footprint? Here are some practical steps we can take:
1. Reduce energy consumption: Opting for renewable energy sources such as solar or wind power, and reducing energy consumption at home and at work, can make a big difference.
2. Sustainable transportation: Using more sustainable modes of transportation, such as walking, cycling, or using public transport instead of driving alone, can significantly reduce carbon emissions.
3. Food choices: Opting for locally sourced and seasonal foods, as well as reducing meat and dairy consumption, can help decrease the carbon footprint associated with food production.
4. Reduce, reuse, recycle: Adopting a minimalist lifestyle and practicing the three Rs principle can help reduce waste and emissions associated with the production and disposal of products.
5. Support sustainable businesses: Choosing to support companies and brands that are committed to environmental sustainability can have a positive impact on reducing the carbon footprint.
It's important to remember that every small action counts in the fight against climate change. By taking steps to reduce our carbon footprint, we're not only protecting the environment but also creating a more sustainable future for future generations.
Together, we can make a difference. 
What will be your next step to reduce your carbon footprint?

Embracing a Circular Economy to Reduce Overconsumption
Shifting from the traditional "take-make-waste" model to a circular economy is essential to curb overconsumption. Central to this approach are the principles of reducing, reusing, and recycling resources. Prioritizing reduction is critical, as the Earth cannot sustain the current levels of resource extraction and use, even with recycling efforts.
Since 1970, global resource use has tripled, leading to significant environmental and social impacts, such as climate change and biodiversity loss. Increasing affluence and population growth are major drivers of this trend. If it continues, resource use could grow by 60% by 2060, far from the goal of halving consumption by 2050.
Reducing overconsumption ensures equitable resource access, as currently, 55% of the global material footprint is consumed by only 26% of the population. Promoting alternatives like sharing and improving material productivity are necessary steps.
Accelerating the closure of material loops is vital. This involves recovering and reusing materials to reduce reliance on virgin resources and mitigate environmental impacts. Increasing recycling rates and using sustainable materials can significantly contribute to this goal. However, current recycling efforts are insufficient, and even in advanced regions like the EU, recycled materials make up only about 11% of total use.
Extending product lifespans is another key aspect, as it reduces the demand for new resources and the emissions associated with production.
Adopting a circular economy is crucial for sustainable resource management and environmental preservation.

I've been reading more and more about the rise of #Repair clinics.  I think this is so smart. Think about all the expensive components that are included in a phone, a computer or a gaming system. If something it stops working, or slows down-- why is our first instinct to get rid of it and buy a new one? 
 
Partially we do this because we've been trained to want the latest and greatest. Partially because new items are cheaper and easier to get than ever.
 
But when we stop & consider repair, instead we are choosing:
1) To reduce landfills
2) To reduce natural resource extraction
3) To support a new repair economy
4) To respect the effort and resource that goes into production and value it as such
5) To reduce greenhouse gas emissions that are warming our planet
AND, as I learned in this article...  6) to create strong social connections within our community
Easier said than done? Maybe. But is it worth a pause & consideration? Absolutely. This article inspired me and I will be paying much more attention to when I can repair vs replace.

Fashion New Balance debuts brand-owned resale channel
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Reddit
By Danny ParisiFeb 5, 2024 
 
New Balance is finally joining the rest of the sneaker industry in getting in on first-party resale. Starting on Monday, the 118-year-old brand is offering New Balance Reconsidered, a program through which customers can exchange their used New Balance sneakers — sent by mail or delivered to a store — for a voucher to use toward their next online purchase. New Balance describes the voucher’s value as “dynamic, based on the seasonality and condition of the product traded in.” Those pre-worn shoes will be sold on New Balance’s online store in a new section of the website labeled Reconsidered.
New Balance is the latest brand to make this move, joining the ranks of other sneaker brands like Nike and Adidas. Over the last two years, brand-owned recommere channels have also been launched by a plethora of non-sneaker brands, including Patagonia, The North Face, Steve Madden, Mara Hoffman and Diane von Furstenberg. While the move toward recommerce began in 2022, 2023 showed that the trend had no signs of stopping. Secondhand fashion grew to be a $20 billion market in the U.S. last year, and it’s likely to keep growing, according to Insider Intelligence. That growth is driven primarily by Gen Z customers.
For New Balance, the launch is as much about sustainability as it is about keeping up with consumer shopping trends. The brand has committed to the Science Based Targets Initiative, which is the United Nations’ emissions reduction initiative that aims to keep global warming under 1.5 degrees Celsius. It’s also planning to reach 100% renewable electricity for its operations by next year.
“We know the footwear industry has a significant environmental impact, including too many products ending up in a landfill,” said John Stokes, director of sustainability at New Balance. “There are many things that have to shift. Launching Reconsidered is one piece of the puzzle, with a program objective to help extend product life for some of our products and get the most from what is already made.”
The platform, which will be promoted through New Balance’s social channels and available on its e-commerce site’s homepage, is powered by Archive, the resale technology company that raised $15 million in funding at the beginning of last year. Archive has signed on a slew of brands over the last year, including Pangaia in September. Other resale service providers like Recurate and Trove have also signed a vast number of brands over the last year. And while no brand-owned resale channel is likely to surpass a third-party marketplace like StockX, which can carry a much larger variety of brands, these channels are often more about brands reclaiming at least a portion of the resale revenue of their products while also keeping customers invested in the brand’s ecosystem.
Emily Gittins, co-founder and CEO of Archive, told Glossy that the interest in opening a resale channel through Archive has “increased exponentially” in the last year. However, Archive, which charges brands both an initial fee and a commission on each sale, has become more selective about which brands it signs on with.
“We have a process of evaluating brands before we sign with them,” Gittins said. “They have to have a quality product that can stand up to being worn many times, and they need to have enough product to have a liquid marketplace. There are a lot of great brands who are interested and want to launch resale one day, but they just don’t have the scale yet.”
New Balance’s other partner in Reconsidered is Tersus Solutions, a textile recycling company that will handle the cleaning and warehousing of all resold New Balance products. The in-store drop-off feature is being piloted at eight New Balance stores across the U.S. 
New Balance is a privately held company and will likely remain so in the future, so it doesn’t report or reveal its annual revenue typically. The last revenue figure publicly available was given last year by managing director Joe Preston, who said the brand’s 2022 revenue was over $5 billion, a 21% increase over the year before. That makes New Balance smaller than Adidas and Nike, which, in terms of revenue, are five- and ten-times larger, respectively. But the number puts New Balance on par with Under Armour, which also sees around $5 billion in annual revenue.
“Offering this ourselves is an important part of taking more responsibility for the products we put into the world and is an important step toward creating a more circular footwear industry,” Stokes said. “We have to start taking steps to learn and adjust. Bigger picture, this focus on longevity and circularity feeds into our ambitious climate goals, which does include finding new ways to generate business value that is not solely dependent on new product creation.”

#CheatSheet: Circular Economy Strategies
🔄 
The global economy faces a major challenge: out of 100 billion tons of materials used annually, only 7.2 billion come from recycled sources. This massive consumption has serious consequences, including health issues, economic losses, and high levels of greenhouse gas emissions.
The blueprint for a sustainable future is embedded within the circular economy, which emphasizes resourcefulness at every stage of the business process. 
Design for Circularity is the foundational step where collaboration with product development teams is essential to create innovative designs that reduce material use and incorporate recycled or sustainably sourced materials. 
This phase also advocates for the use of safer chemicals and designs products for increased durability, repairability, and recyclability. It rethinks the product lifecycle right from conception to ensure that every stage is optimized for minimal waste.
Procurement is another critical pillar in the circular economy. It calls for intentional sourcing, favoring bio-based or recycled materials that divert waste from landfills. Upcycling waste into new products not only adds value but also preserves quality. 
This approach demands a close partnership with suppliers to secure materials that meet circular principles, ensuring that the materials used in production contribute to a regenerative economic system.
Manufacturing and operational processes are reimagined to prioritize efficiency and minimize waste. 
By optimizing material flows and energy use, companies can lean towards more sustainable production methods. The adaptation of make-to-order models and improvement in forecasting help to limit overproduction and excess inventory, which in turn reduces waste. 
When products reach the end of their life cycle, strategies such as remanufacturing, refurbishing, and recycling come into play to ensure that the materials are re-entered into the production cycle, thus maintaining the loop of circularity.
In the shift towards a more circular economy, every company plays a part. By adopting circular strategies, businesses can lead the way to a sustainable and environmentally responsible future.
Source: Environmental Defense Fund
